```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, dpi = 96
)
library(fdachange)

# Colorblind-safe categorical palette (validated adjacent-pair order);
# assignments are fixed per entity across every figure in this vignette.
pal <- c(blue = "#2a78d6", orange = "#eb6834", aqua = "#1baf7a",
         yellow = "#eda100")
col_changed  <- pal[["blue"]]     # curves / cells inside the change window
col_plain    <- "grey75"          # unchanged curves, recessive marks
col_band     <- adjustcolor("grey50", 0.18)  # true-window shading (annotation)
proj_col <- c(l2 = pal[["blue"]], ito = pal[["orange"]],
              c_max_var = pal[["aqua"]], pc1 = pal[["yellow"]])

has_fda <- requireNamespace("fda", quietly = TRUE)
has_usc <- has_fda && requireNamespace("fda.usc", quietly = TRUE)

shade_window <- function(from, to, n) {
  usr <- par("usr")
  rect(from, usr[3], to, usr[4], col = col_band, border = NA)
}
```

## The epidemic alternative

An *epidemic* (changed-segment) alternative means a sample
$X_1, \dots, X_n$ is i.i.d. except on an unknown window
$I^\ast = \{k^\ast + 1, \dots, k^\ast + l^\ast\}$, where the distribution
changes and then changes back. fdachange implements four weighted scan
tests for this alternative:

| Test | Function | Sensitive to |
|---|---|---|
| Wilcoxon-type antisymmetric-kernel scan | `wilcoxon_statistic()` | location (`h_w`) or scale/tail (`h_0`) changes |
| Lp empirical-process scan | `lp_statistic()` | general distributional change |
| RKHS kernel mean-embedding scan | `rkhs_statistic()` | general distributional change |
| Birbilas CUSUM-type functional statistic | `far1_statistic()` | functional mean jumps under FAR(1) dependence |

Each scan weights a window of relative length $t$ by the Hoelder-type
weight $w(t) = t^{-\gamma} \log(c/t)^{-\beta}$: larger $\gamma$
up-weights short windows, at the price of heavier-tailed null
distributions.

```{r weights, fig.height = 3.2}
t <- seq(0.005, 0.995, length.out = 400)
gammas <- c(0, 0.25, 0.45)
w <- sapply(gammas, function(g) holder_weight(t * (1 - t), g))
matplot(t, w, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2, col = pal[1:3], bty = "l",
        xlab = "relative window length l/n",
        ylab = "symmetric weight w(t(1-t))", ylim = c(0, 12))
text(0.06, w[20, ] + 0.6, labels = paste0("gamma = ", gammas),
     col = pal[1:3], adj = 0, cex = 0.9)
legend("topright", legend = paste0("gamma = ", gammas), col = pal[1:3],
       lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.9)
```

## Quick start: a scalar series

`generate_s1()` draws an i.i.d. N(0, 1) series with an epidemic mean
shift on a chosen window; `epidemic_test()` runs a calibrated test and
localizes the change.

```{r quickstart}
set.seed(1)
x <- generate_s1(200, a = 1, ec_interval = c(0.4, 0.7))
ht <- epidemic_test(x, method = "wilcoxon", gamma = 0.25)
ht
```

```{r quickstart-plot, fig.height = 3.6}
plot(x, type = "l", col = col_plain, lwd = 1, bty = "l",
     xlab = "observation index", ylab = "x")
shade_window(80.5, 140.5, 200)              # true window I* = {81..140}
lines(81:140, x[81:140], col = col_changed, lwd = 1.4)
abline(v = c(ht$k + 1, ht$m), lty = 2, lwd = 2)
text(mean(c(ht$k + 1, ht$m)), max(x), "detected window", cex = 0.9)
legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", cex = 0.9,
       legend = c("changed segment (truth, shaded)", "detected (dashed)"),
       col = c(col_changed, "black"), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = c(1.4, 2))
```

The shaded band is the true window; the dashed lines are the window the
scan reports (`ht$k + 1` to `ht$m`, the thesis convention
$I(k, m) = \{k+1, \dots, m\}$).

## Functional data and the benchmark scenarios

The functional scenarios return a matrix with one curve per column,
sampled on `l + 1` grid points. `generate_f1()` puts centred-Pareto
coefficients on a cosine basis inside the window; `generate_f5()` adds a
spike to i.i.d. Wiener (random-walk) curves.

```{r curves, fig.height = 3.8}
set.seed(2)
n <- 60
X1 <- generate_f1(n, a = 3)
X5 <- generate_f5(n, a = 4)
s  <- seq(0, 1, length.out = nrow(X5))
win <- 25:42                                # exact window at n = 60
old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
matplot(s, X1, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 0.7, col = col_plain, bty = "l",
        xlab = "t", ylab = "X(t)", main = "F1: heavy-tailed coefficients")
matlines(s, X1[, win], lty = 1, lwd = 0.9, col = col_changed)
matplot(s, X5, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 0.7, col = col_plain, bty = "l",
        xlab = "t", ylab = "X(t)", main = "F5: Wiener + spike")
matlines(s, X5[, win], lty = 1, lwd = 0.9, col = col_changed)
par(old)
```

Blue curves are the ones inside the change window. F5's spike is the
dissertation's spike function
$f_\alpha(t) = (1 - |t - 1/2|^\alpha)^{1/\alpha}$, a Hoelder-$\alpha$
cusp at $t = 1/2$ (default `spike_alpha = 0.45`):

```{r falpha, fig.height = 3.2}
f_alpha <- function(t, al) (1 - abs(t - 0.5)^al)^(1 / al)
alphas <- c(0.45, 0.3, 0.15)
tt <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 401)
fa <- sapply(alphas, f_alpha, t = tt)
matplot(tt, fa, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2, col = pal[1:3], bty = "l",
        xlab = "t", ylab = expression(f[alpha](t)))
legend("topright", legend = paste0("alpha = ", alphas), col = pal[1:3],
       lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.9)
```

## Projections visualized

The scalar scans consume a numeric series, so functional data is first
reduced by a projection. Different projections preserve different
aspects of the change; the color of each projection is fixed throughout
this vignette.

`project_l2()` (deterministic, the $L_2$ norm of each curve) and
`project_ito()` (integral against one shared random Wiener path per
call) need only base R:

```{r proj-base, fig.height = 3.8}
set.seed(3)
p_l2  <- project_l2(X5)
p_ito <- project_ito(X5)
old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (nm in c("l2", "ito")) {
  p <- if (nm == "l2") p_l2 else p_ito
  plot(p, type = "b", pch = 16, cex = 0.7, lwd = 1.2, col = proj_col[[nm]],
       bty = "l", xlab = "curve index", ylab = "projected value",
       main = paste0("project_", nm))
  shade_window(24.5, 42.5, n)
}
par(old)
```

The point-evaluation style projection `project_c_max_var()` (evaluate
every curve at a randomly chosen critical point of the variance
function) and `project_pc1()` (inner product with the leading functional
principal component) use the fda / fda.usc basis machinery:

```{r proj-usc, eval = has_usc, fig.height = 3.8}
set.seed(4)
p_cmv <- project_c_max_var(X5)
p_pc1 <- project_pc1(X5)
old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (nm in c("c_max_var", "pc1")) {
  p <- if (nm == "c_max_var") p_cmv else p_pc1
  plot(p, type = "b", pch = 16, cex = 0.7, lwd = 1.2, col = proj_col[[nm]],
       bty = "l", xlab = "curve index", ylab = "projected value",
       main = paste0("project_", nm))
  shade_window(24.5, 42.5, n)
}
par(old)
```

At this spike amplitude several projections separate the window: the
point-evaluation `c_max_var` because the variance-critical point lands
on the spike, and the norm `l2` because a bump of height 4 moves the
whole curve's norm. The projection whose random direction can simply
miss the spike (`ito`) shows the weakest separation - and the full power
study below confirms that ordering, with the point-evaluation advantage
concentrated at *faint* amplitudes where the norm barely moves. The
stochastic projections (`ito`, `c_max_var`, `wiener`) draw a fresh
random direction on every call; `scan_over_splits()` exploits exactly
that to aggregate independent chunks (the paper-1 $T^{(d)}$ statistic).

## Testing, localization, calibration

Every method runs through the same `epidemic_test()` interface. On the
projected F5 series (a larger sample this time so the asymptotic
calibration is comfortable):

```{r tests}
set.seed(5)
Xb <- generate_f5(200, a = 3)
xb <- project_l2(Xb)
res <- lapply(c("wilcoxon", "lp", "rkhs"), function(m) {
  ht <- epidemic_test(xb, m, gamma = 0.25)
  data.frame(method = m, statistic = unname(ht$statistic),
             critical = ht$critical.value, p.value = ht$p.value,
             window = sprintf("[%d, %d]", ht$k + 1, ht$m))
})
do.call(rbind, res)
```

Calibration is resolved automatically, in this order:

1. **Closed form** where it exists: the Wilcoxon scan at $\gamma = 0$ is
   calibrated by Kuiper's law, exactly
   (`kuiper_quantile(0.95)` = `r round(kuiper_quantile(0.95), 4)`).
2. **Shipped Monte-Carlo caches** for the published
   (gamma, kernel, p) cells: `wilcoxon_null_draws()`, `lp_null_draws()`,
   `rkhs_null_draws()`, `far1_null_draws()`.
3. **Your own draws** for anything else - simulate, then either pass via
   `epidemic_test(null = )` or store for automatic lookup:

```{r simulate-null, eval = FALSE}
# store into a throwaway cache dir if you are only experimenting
options(fdachange.cache_dir = tempfile("fdachange-cache-"))
draws <- simulate_wilcoxon_null(1000, gamma = 0.1, grid = 2000, cores = 4)
save_null_draws(draws, "wilcoxon", gamma = 0.1)
wilcoxon_critical_value(0.1)   # now served from your draws
```

One caveat worth repeating from the reference pages: the Wilcoxon scan
and the ecdf-path Lp scan are rank-based, so their nulls apply to any
continuous data. The RKHS caches are tied to the H0 distribution named
by their `baseline` tag - for other marginals, simulate with
`simulate_rkhs_null(rdist = ...)`.

## A small power simulation

A miniature version of the spike experiment: does the projection choice
matter for detecting a faint spike? (Small `n` and `N_rep` keep this
chunk fast; the full study is described below.)

```{r mini-power, fig.height = 3.6}
set.seed(42)
a_grid <- c(0, 1, 2, 4)
n_rep  <- 30L
cv <- wilcoxon_critical_value(0.25)
power <- sapply(c("l2", "ito"), function(nm) {
  proj <- projection_fn(nm)
  sapply(a_grid, function(a) {
    mean(replicate(n_rep, {
      X <- generate_f5(100, a = a)
      wilcoxon_statistic(proj(X), 0.25, kernel = "h_0") > cv
    }))
  })
})
matplot(a_grid, power, type = "b", pch = 16, lty = 1, lwd = 2,
        col = proj_col[c("l2", "ito")], bty = "l", ylim = c(0, 1),
        xlab = "spike amplitude a", ylab = "rejection rate")
abline(h = 0.05, col = col_plain, lty = 3)
legend("topleft", legend = c("project_l2", "project_ito"),
       col = proj_col[c("l2", "ito")], lwd = 2, pch = 16, bty = "n")
```

The committed full-scale study (`reproduction/data/f5_spike_power.csv`:
n = 400, N_rep = 100, corrected Wilcoxon and Lp scans over c_max_var /
l2 / ito) gives the complete picture, and its verdict is nuanced: the
point-evaluation projection `c_max_var` is the most powerful for *faint*
spikes (for the Lp scan at a = 0.5 - 1 it reaches 2 - 3 times the power
of `l2`) and has the best mean power overall for Lp (0.46 vs 0.41 / 0.40),
but it is not uniformly dominant - at large amplitudes the norm
projections catch up, and for the Wilcoxon h_0 scan `l2` wins on
average. Regenerate it with `reproduction/sweeps/run_f5_spike_power.sh`.

## An application-shaped analysis

The dissertation's application scans weekly electricity balancing-price
curves (168 hourly points per week). Its preprocessing step matters:
curves are first reconstructed on the level-$K$ Faber-Schauder
(order-2 B-spline) space. `reconstruct()` exposes that step; here it is
on the spike function sampled with noise, the vignette-sized version of
the dissertation's smoothing figure:

```{r reconstruct, fig.height = 3.6}
set.seed(6)
t_in <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 168)
y <- f_alpha(t_in, 0.45) + rnorm(168, 0, 0.05)
Y <- matrix(y, ncol = 1)
r2 <- reconstruct(Y, method = "fs_interp", K = 2)
r4 <- reconstruct(Y, method = "fs_interp", K = 4)
plot(t_in, y, type = "l", col = col_plain, lwd = 1, bty = "l",
     xlab = "t", ylab = "curve", main = "Faber-Schauder truncation")
lines(r2$argvals, r2$X[, 1], col = pal[["orange"]], lwd = 2)
lines(r4$argvals, r4$X[, 1], col = pal[["blue"]], lwd = 2)
legend("topright", bty = "n", cex = 0.9, lwd = c(1, 2, 2),
       col = c(col_plain, pal[["orange"]], pal[["blue"]]),
       legend = c("sampled curve (168 pts)", "fs_interp, K = 2",
                  "fs_interp, K = 4"))
```

The full pipeline on application-shaped synthetic data - weekly-sized
curves, reconstruct, project, test:

```{r app-pipeline}
set.seed(7)
Xw <- generate_f5(150, a = 3, l = 167)        # 168-point grid, like a week
rec <- reconstruct(Xw, method = "fs_interp", K = 4)
epidemic_test(project_l2(rec$X), "wilcoxon", gamma = 0.25)
```

On the real data (345 weeks, fixed data pipeline, outlier week removed;
raw exports are fetched and checksum-verified by
`reproduction/applications/litgrid/download_litgrid.R`), the corrected
scans reject at every considered gamma. A few rows of the committed
result table (`reproduction/data/litgrid_corrected_tables.csv`):

```{r app-table, echo = FALSE}
app <- data.frame(
  method     = c("wilcoxon", "wilcoxon", "lp", "lp", "wilcoxon", "lp"),
  projection = c("l2", "l2", "l2", "l2", "c_max_var", "c_max_var"),
  gamma      = c(0.25, 0.45, 0.25, 0.45, 0.45, 0.45),
  statistic  = c(8.32, 10.98, 2.30, 2.78, 13.11, 3.43),
  critical   = c(2.538, 3.851, 0.683, 1.082, 3.851, 1.082),
  window     = c("[0.078, 0.603]", "[0.078, 0.603]", "[0.197, 0.603]",
                 "[0.316, 0.603]", "[0.003, 0.603]", "[0.603, 1.000]")
)
knitr::kable(app, caption = paste(
  "Corrected application results, fixed pipeline, no outlier (n = 345).",
  "Every cell rejects at the 5% level."))
```

The detected windows agree on the segment end near the 60% mark of the
sample - the energy-crisis period the dissertation's application chapter
discusses.
